title: The Fourth Street School to Mount Herzl: the Kibbutz, the Ministries, and the War of Atonement
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Kyiv, born in the Pale
stops.date_confidence: Date and city attested (Wikipedia, Golda Meir; MSU Denver chronology). The article says only downtown Kiev; the Podil attribution carried in an earlier dossier is unsupported and dropped here, along with its coordinate, which sat about 2.5 km north of downtown. The pin is the memorial plaque at 5-A Baseina Street in Lypky, the only documented address associated with her birth, not a verified birth house. Old Style, the date is 21 April 1898.
stops.campa: Goldie Mabovitch is born in downtown Kyiv on the third of May, into a poor Yiddish-speaking household in an empire where a Jew requires a permit for nearly everything. Her father Moshe is a carpenter whose work does not hold. The household is counted for tax and for restriction like every other Jewish household in the Pale. No surviving record names the room or the street. What the city keeps instead is a plaque screwed to a wall on Baseina Street, put up long after she was famous, saying that she began here.
suggested_refs: The memorial plaque at 5-A Baseina Street, Kyiv

stops.name: Pinsk, the father gone ahead
stops.date_confidence: The move to Pinsk and Moshe Mabovitch's departure for the United States are attested by the MSU Denver chronology, which gives 1903. Month and day are not recorded and default to 01. The Pinsk coordinate is the town, not a residence.
stops.campa: The carpentry fails and the family goes north to Pinsk, to her mother's people, while Moshe sails for America to find work that will pay for tickets. Three years pass in the interval between one country and another: a mother, three daughters, a household kept on credit and on letters. Her father becomes a signature and a promise of tickets. Her elder sister Sheyna is already meeting with young socialists in rooms the police would raid if they knew, and Golda, five years old, sits at the edge of the room and listens.
suggested_refs: The Jewish quarter of Pinsk before the First World War

stops.name: Quebec City, the landing
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia (Golda Meir) confirms that Blume Mabovitch and her daughters landed at Quebec in 1906 en route to Milwaukee. The month, the ship, and the pier are not documented in any source reachable here; the date defaults to 01 and the pin is the port city.
stops.campa: Blume Mabovitch comes ashore in Canada with three daughters and the language of none of it. They are processed, counted, and put on a train south and west, across a continent whose scale nobody in Pinsk had described to them, toward a father who has been a signature on letters for three years. Golda is eight. The crossing was steerage and the food was bad and the papers were in order. The train takes days. The reunion is in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, in a rented flat above a shop.
suggested_refs: Passenger records of the port of Quebec, 1906

stops.name: Milwaukee, the Fourth Street School
stops.date_confidence: Attendance 1906-1912 and graduation as valedictorian in 1912 are attested (Wikipedia, Golda Meir School), as are the 1979 renaming and the 1990 National Historic Landmark designation. The 1908 American Young Sisters Society is attested by the MSU Denver chronology. The coordinate is the building's own, at 1555 N Dr Martin Luther King Jr Drive; an earlier dossier put it 1.4 km north and a second put it 1.4 km south, and neither was right. Month defaults to 01.
stops.campa: She enters an American grade school in 1906 unable to read the alphabet on the board, and leaves it in 1912 at the head of the class, as valedictorian. At ten she discovers that the school supplies no textbooks and that the poorest children therefore sit without them, so she founds the American Young Sisters Society with her friend Regina Hamburger, rents a hall, prints handbills, and asks the neighbourhood for money from a platform, having written no speech. The hall is full.
suggested_refs: The Golda Meir School, 1555 N Dr Martin Luther King Jr Drive, Milwaukee, renamed 1979 and designated a National Historic Landmark in 1990

stops.name: Milwaukee, North Division High School
stops.date_confidence: Entry in 1912 and completion in 1915 are attested (Wikipedia, Golda Meir; MSU Denver chronology). The coordinate is North Division High School as it stands, in a building opened in September 1978 just east of the old site; the building Meir attended stood elsewhere and its address was not established in any source reachable here. Month defaults to 01.
stops.campa: She enters high school against her mother's judgement and pays for it by working: the counter at Schuster's department store, hours at the public library, evenings helping in the family's small grocery before school opens. Blume Mabovitch has a different plan, which is a husband nearly twice her daughter's age and an end to books. The argument runs for months in a kitchen where both women are certain, and it does not resolve. It is settled instead by a letter to Denver and a railway ticket bought in secret.
suggested_refs: North Division High School, Milwaukee, records of 1912-1915

stops.name: Denver, the house on Julian Street
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the address. The Auraria Campus history of the Golda Meir House gives 1606-1608 Julian Street as the original site and the Korngold household as her refuge in 1913-1914; the house was moved to 1301 S Lipan Street on the Auraria campus in 1988, so the pin is an estimate for the original Julian Street lot and not the building where it now stands. The flight from Milwaukee and its cause are attested by the MSU Denver chronology.
stops.campa: At fourteen she runs away to her sister Sheyna, who is recovering from tuberculosis in a West Denver duplex, and finds the household is also a salon. Anarchists, Bundists, Labour Zionists and suffragists come through the front room and argue past midnight over tea nobody pays for, and the runaway sits in the corner of it night after night, listening to grown people take ideas seriously enough to break with each other over them. She is fourteen. In that room she meets a sign painter with a taste for poetry named Morris Meyerson.
stops.quote: to the extent that my own future convictions were shaped and given form, and ideas were discarded or accepted by me while I was growing up, those talk-filled nights in Denver played a considerable role.
stops.quote_source: Golda Meir, My Life, quoted on the MSU Denver chronology page
suggested_refs: The Golda Meir House, moved in 1988 from 1606-1608 Julian Street to 1301 S Lipan Street, Auraria Campus, Denver
sources: Auraria Campus, Golda Meir House history

stops.name: Denver, North High School
stops.date_confidence: The enrolment date of 17 February 1913 is given by the MSU Denver chronology. The coordinate is North High School at 2960 N Speer Boulevard (Wikipedia, North High School (Colorado)); the Beaux-Arts building was completed in 1911 and still forms the core of the school, so this is the building she entered. An earlier dossier called the campus unverified and placed it 700 m southeast; both claims were wrong.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of February she enrols, a runaway with no money and a sister's spare room, and the Denver year becomes the one she names ever afterwards when asked where she was made. She works part of the day and attends class the rest, and argues at night in a front room where nobody defers to her age. Within a year she has quarrelled with Sheyna over housekeeping and independence, moved into a room of her own, and kept herself on day work of whatever kind was going. She stays in school throughout.
stops.quote: Denver was a turning point because my real education began. In Denver, life really opened up for me.
stops.quote_source: Golda Meir, My Life, quoted on the MSU Denver chronology page
suggested_refs: North High School, 2960 N Speer Boulevard, Denver, opened 1911

stops.name: Milwaukee, the Normal School and the Folks Schule
stops.date_confidence: Contested span. The MSU Denver chronology says she attended the Wisconsin State Normal School for a year from 1916 and taught at a Yiddish Folks Schule; the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee states that she graduated from the Milwaukee State Normal School in 1917, which is the stated reason its main library carries her name. The span is given here as 1916-1917 with graduation in 1917. The Normal School building's location was not established in any source reachable here, so the pin is the Mabovitch family's Milwaukee, not the campus.
stops.campa: Her parents write asking her to come home, and this time the terms are hers: she returns to Milwaukee, finishes high school, and trains as a teacher at the state normal school. She joins Poale Zion and speaks for it on street corners, standing on a box, in English and in Yiddish, until her father stops threatening to drag her home by the braid and comes instead to listen. Afternoons she teaches Yiddish reading and Jewish history at a Folks Schule, to the children of immigrants who arrived after her.
suggested_refs: The Golda Meir Library, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, named for her 1917 graduation from the Milwaukee State Normal School

stops.name: Milwaukee, the wedding and its condition
stops.date_confidence: The date and the household are attested by the MSU Denver chronology, which also records that her father became a United States citizen in July 1917. The condition she attached to the marriage is attested by Wikipedia (Golda Meir). The exact address of the Mabovitch home was not documented in any source reachable here, so the pin is city-level.
stops.campa: She marries Morris Meyerson on Christmas Eve in her parents' front room, under a canopy, having told him plainly what she will require: not a house in Milwaukee but a passage to Palestine and a life on the land. He does not want it. He wants concerts, books, a quiet job, a wife who reads with him in the evening. He agrees because he wants her more than he wants any of that. Her father has taken American citizenship five months earlier, in July. The passage they have just agreed on takes another four years to arrange.
suggested_refs: Marriage record of Golda Mabovitch and Morris Meyerson, Milwaukee, 24 December 1917

stops.name: Port of New York, sailing on the Pocahontas
stops.date_confidence: The ship, the port of departure, the Naples leg and the travelling party (Sheyna's family and Regina Hamburger among them) are attested by Wikipedia (Golda Meir) and the MSU Denver chronology. Only the year is fixed; month and day default to 01. The pin is the New York waterfront, not an identified pier.
stops.campa: The SS Pocahontas sails for Naples with the Meyersons aboard, Sheyna and her children, and Regina Hamburger from the Fourth Street School. Golda is twenty-three and has been arguing for this passage since she was fifteen. She leaves behind a teaching certificate, a family, and a movement that has already learned to send her out to raise money because she can hold a room. The crew mutinies before the Mediterranean and the engines fail more than once.
suggested_refs: Sailing records of the SS Pocahontas, New York to Naples, 1921

stops.name: Naples, transferring for Palestine
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia (Golda Meir) states that the Pocahontas sailed from New York to Naples and that the party went on from there overland to Tel Aviv. Only the year is attested; month and day default to 01. The pin is the port of Naples; no berth or hotel is named in the sources reachable here.
stops.campa: The party comes off the ship in Italy and waits among trunks on a foreign quay for the onward leg, which will be made by rail and not by sea. Behind them are an American passport, a paid teaching post, and a mother who begged her not to go. Ahead is a mandate territory administered by Britain, malarial in its valleys, where the work waiting for her has not been described to her accurately by anyone. Regina Hamburger, who helped her rent a hall in Milwaukee at ten years old to buy other children their schoolbooks, is sitting on the next trunk.
suggested_refs: The port of Naples as a transit point for Third Aliyah passages, 1921

stops.name: Kibbutz Merhavia, rejected and then admitted
stops.date_confidence: Arrival at Tel Aviv by train and the initial rejection then acceptance at Merhavia are attested (Wikipedia, Golda Meir; MSU Denver chronology). The coordinate is confirmed exactly by Wikipedia, Merhavia (kibbutz). The apparent conflict with a 1929 founding date resolves rather than standing: Merhavia the moshav was established in 1911 and Merhavia the kibbutz was founded beside it in 1929, so the collective she joined in 1921 was the earlier settlement. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: They come up from the Tel Aviv train to the Jezreel Valley and apply to a collective that does not want them: Americans, the members say, soft, and worse, a married couple, and worse again, a wife who will want a primus stove of her own. She is voted down and applies again and is admitted. She picks almonds, plants saplings, cleans the chicken coops nobody wants, and reorganises the communal kitchen so that the porridge is edible and the oats are served with the milk. Within two years the kibbutz sends her to the Histadrut as its delegate.
suggested_refs: Merhavia in the Jezreel Valley, the 1911 settlement and the 1929 kibbutz founded beside it

stops.name: Jerusalem, the years of the two children
stops.date_confidence: Menachem's birth in 1924 and Sara's in Jerusalem in 1926 are attested by the MSU Denver chronology, as is a brief return to Merhavia in 1925, which that chronology alone reports. No residential address is documented in any source reachable here, so the pin is city-level Jerusalem. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Morris will not stay on the kibbutz and his health will not let him, so they leave it, and the promise made in Milwaukee is spent. In Jerusalem there is a basement flat, an irregular wage from bookkeeping, a son born in 1924 and a daughter in 1926, laundry done in exchange for the children's nursery fees, and no money for kerosene in winter. She takes in washing and hates it. When the Histadrut offers her office work she takes that too. They will live apart for most of what is left to them, and they never divorce.
suggested_refs: The Meyerson household in Jerusalem, 1924-1928

stops.name: Tel Aviv, secretary of the Working Women's Council
stops.date_confidence: The appointment as secretary of Mo'etzet Ha-Po'alot, the Histadrut's Working Women's Council, and the move to Tel Aviv are attested by the MSU Denver chronology, which gives 1928. Month and day default to 01. The Council's offices are not located in any source reachable here; the pin is Tel Aviv.
stops.campa: At thirty she is given the Working Women's Council, with a brief that runs from agricultural training farms for girls to childcare for women working the fields. She moves the children to Tel Aviv. The office sends her abroad constantly, to America, to England, to congresses in Europe, and Menachem and Sara spend a good part of their childhood writing to her. The argument she starts making in this job she will go on making for forty years: a woman in this country is not to be provided for, she is to be employed.
suggested_refs: Mo'etzet Ha-Po'alot, the Histadrut Working Women's Council, records of 1928-1934

stops.name: New York, the emissary and the sick child
stops.date_confidence: The 1932 return to the United States as a Histadrut and Pioneer Women emissary, and her daughter Sara's kidney illness as a reason for the journey, are attested by the MSU Denver chronology; election to the Histadrut Executive Committee on her return in 1934 is attested by the same source. The tour is not itemized by city in any source reachable here, so the pin is New York, her port of arrival, and month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: She returns to America on two errands that happen to point the same way: raise money for the Histadrut among Jewish women who have never seen the Jezreel Valley, and get her daughter into a hospital that can treat a failing kidney. For two years she crosses the country speaking in synagogue basements and union halls, in Yiddish and in English, on whatever platform Pioneer Women can find for her. Sara is treated and recovers. In 1934 she sails back and is elected to the Histadrut Executive Committee.
suggested_refs: Pioneer Women, the Women's Labor Zionist Organization of America, speaking tours of 1932-1934

stops.name: Evian-les-Bains, the observer who may not speak
stops.date_confidence: The conference ran 6 to 15 July 1938 at the Hotel Royal, and Meir's attendance as the Jewish observer from Palestine, barred from speaking and from sitting with the delegates, is attested by Wikipedia (Evian Conference), which also quotes her own description of the role. The pin is the Hotel Royal on the hillside above the town, roughly 1.5 km south-southwest of the lakefront centre, where an earlier dossier had wrongly placed it.
stops.campa: Thirty-two nations meet at a lakeside hotel in Savoy to discuss what is to be done about the Jews of Germany and Austria, and one after another explain, in the courteous language of the period, that their own countries are full. She is present as an observer from Palestine and is not permitted to address them or to sit among them. She sits in the gallery for ten days and listens to it in three languages, and when it is over she says one sentence to the press.
stops.quote: There is only one thing I hope to see before I die and that is that my people should not need expressions of sympathy anymore.
stops.quote_source: Golda Meir to the press at the Evian Conference, 1938, quoted on the MSU Denver chronology page
suggested_refs: The Hotel Royal, Evian-les-Bains, venue of the conference of 6-15 July 1938

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Jewish Agency after the Black Sabbath
stops.date_confidence: Operation Agatha of 29 June 1946 and her succession to the head of the Jewish Agency's Political Department, first acting and then full, are attested by the MSU Denver chronology and corroborated by Wikipedia (Golda Meir). The coordinate is the Jewish Agency headquarters at 48 King George Street; an earlier dossier placed it 400 m southeast, nearer Zion Square.
stops.campa: British troops seal the country on a Saturday morning and arrest the leadership of the Yishuv in their beds, Moshe Sharett among them, and the Political Department of the Jewish Agency is left in the hands of the one senior figure the Mandate did not think worth detaining. She takes the desk. For two years she negotiates with the administration that jailed her colleagues, over immigration certificates, over detainees, over curfews, over the ships turned back off the coast. She conducts all of it in English. She holds the department until the Mandate ends.
suggested_refs: The Jewish Agency building, 48 King George Street, Jerusalem

stops.name: Cyprus, the camps at Caraolos
stops.date_confidence: The 1947 visit to Jewish detainees interned on Cyprus is attested by Wikipedia (Golda Meir). What is not corroborated is the narrative of persuasion: Wikipedia's article on the Cyprus internment camps does not mention Meir, and records instead a British-set quota of 750 certificates a month from November 1946 with special allocations decided by the British for pregnant women, nursing mothers and the elderly. The claim that she persuaded detainees to yield their places to families is a reconstruction. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Behind British wire near Famagusta sit tens of thousands of Jews taken off ships intercepted between Europe and Palestine, most of them out of camps that had already held them once. The immigration certificates the administration issues are counted in hundreds a month against a population counted in tens of thousands. She goes over to see it, walks the compounds, and comes back into the argument over who is to be let in first with the numbers in her own handwriting. Who decided the order of that queue is what the record disagrees about.
suggested_refs: The Caraolos and Dhekelia internment camps, Cyprus, 1946-1949

stops.name: Naharayim, the first meeting with Abdullah
stops.date_confidence: Attested verbatim: Wikipedia (Naharayim) states that Naharayim was the venue for a meeting between Golda Meir and King Abdullah on 17 November 1947. The date corrects a bare 1947 carried in an earlier dossier.
stops.campa: Ten days before the United Nations votes on partition, she is driven to the hydroelectric works at Naharayim, where the Yarmouk meets the Jordan, to meet the King of Transjordan in a room lent by the power company. The proposition is simple and is never written down: the Arab Legion is the only Arab army worth the name, and if it stays out of the coming war the Jewish state will not contest the King's claim to the rest of Palestine. Abdullah is agreeable. He is also a client of the British, who train and pay his army.
suggested_refs: The Naharayim power station on the Jordan, venue of the meeting of 17 November 1947

stops.name: Chicago, the speech that buys the arms
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia (Golda Meir) dates the first delivery of the emotional appeal to Chicago on 22 January 1948 and gives the total raised as over 30 million dollars. That the venue was the Council of Jewish Federations and Welfare Funds is not corroborated by that source and is left hedged here. The car accident that injured her later in the same American mission is attested only by the MSU Denver chronology, without date or place.
stops.campa: Ben-Gurion means to go to America himself to ask for money and she tells him to stay and run the war, because she can do the asking. She lands in a winter coat borrowed from her daughter, with no prepared text, and speaks to a hall of American Jewish community leaders in Chicago on the twenty-second of January: the decision whether we live or die is yours, the fighting we will do ourselves. She goes on speaking city after city until a car accident puts her in hospital. The tour raises over thirty million dollars. The money buys rifles from Czechoslovakia.
stops.quote: The thing that mattered most in my life was that if a thing has to be done, you don't waste time with theories and debates. You just do it.
stops.quote_source: Golda Meir, remark to a friend, quoted on the MSU Denver chronology page under 1948
suggested_refs: The Chicago appeal of 22 January 1948 and the American fundraising tour that followed

stops.name: Haifa, the city after the Haganah takes it
stops.date_confidence: The visit to Haifa after its capture by the Haganah is attested among the dated entries of Wikipedia (Golda Meir). The quote carried here is traced verbatim to the MSU Denver chronology at its 1948 entry, where it is attributed to My Life; the occasion of the remark is not fixed by that source and it should not be read as spoken in Haifa. An earlier dossier reproduced it with a comma in place of the source's dash.
stops.campa: She walks through a port city whose Arab population, some seventy thousand people, has largely left it in the weeks since the Haganah took the lower town on the twenty-second of April. She goes into houses with the meals still on the tables and the doors standing open. Three months earlier she was in Chicago raising the money that armed the men who took this town, and she had told the hall the fighting would be done at home. What she writes about the houses afterwards does not resolve into consolation.
stops.quote: One's duty was one duty – and it had nothing to do with justice.
stops.quote_source: Golda Meir, My Life, quoted on the MSU Denver chronology page under 1948; the occasion of the remark is not given by that source
suggested_refs: Haifa in the weeks after 22 April 1948

stops.name: Amman, the second meeting, in disguise
stops.date_confidence: The clandestine journey to Amman on 10 May 1948, made in disguise, is attested by the MSU Denver chronology and corroborated by Wikipedia (Naharayim), which places it after the Gesher incident. The quote is traced verbatim to the MSU Denver chronology, which specifies that it was said to Abdullah at the secret meeting in Amman; popular accounts split between this meeting and the Naharayim meeting of November 1947, and that ambiguity is left standing here rather than resolved.
stops.campa: Four days before the Mandate expires she crosses the Jordan dressed as an Arab woman, veiled, in a car driven through Legion checkpoints, and is brought to the King. He is no longer agreeable. He offers autonomy for the Jews inside a Hashemite kingdom and says she is in too much of a hurry. She answers him with a sentence about two thousand years and comes back over the river certain that the Legion will fight, and says so to the Provisional Council in the plainest terms available.
stops.quote: We have been waiting for 2,000 years. Is that hurrying?
stops.quote_source: Golda Meir to King Abdullah I at their secret meeting in Amman, 1948, quoted on the MSU Denver chronology page
suggested_refs: The secret Amman meeting of 10 May 1948

stops.name: Tel Aviv, signing the Declaration at 16 Rothschild Boulevard
stops.date_confidence: The venue, its address and its coordinate are attested by Wikipedia (Independence Hall, Israel). That Meir was one of thirty-seven signatories and one of two women is attested by the MSU Denver chronology and is documented in the Knesset's published signatory list; the fetched Wikipedia excerpt for the hall itself did not name her.
stops.campa: In the small museum hall on Rothschild Boulevard, at four in the afternoon on a Friday, before the Sabbath and before the Mandate's last hours run out, thirty-seven people sign a page declaring a state. She is one of two women who sign it. She is photographed weeping and is asked about it afterwards and says that she thought of the ones who were not there to see it. Egyptian aircraft bomb the city within a day, and she is already booked on a flight to New York to raise more money.
suggested_refs: Independence Hall, 16 Rothschild Boulevard, Tel Aviv, and the Knesset's published list of the thirty-seven signatories

segments.name: Moscow and the Ministry of Labour

stops.name: Moscow, the crowd outside the Choral Synagogue
stops.date_confidence: Her arrival in Moscow as Israel's first minister plenipotentiary in September 1948 is attested by the MSU Denver chronology, with the Jewish Virtual Library dating the appointment to June 1948. The synagogue scene is attested by Wikipedia (Moscow Choral Synagogue), at 10 Bolshoy Spasoglinishchevsky Lane, whose coordinate is used here; the Bolshaya Bronnaya attribution in an earlier dossier belongs to a different Moscow synagogue and is struck. Rosh Hashanah 5709 fell on 4-5 October 1948, so the date given elsewhere as 3 October is likely the eve. Only the Rosh Hashanah appearance is documented; a separate Yom Kippur appearance is not.
stops.campa: She arrives in Moscow as the first minister of a state three months old, to a country where Jewish institutions have been closed, Yiddish schools shut, and the word Zionist is an indictment. On the new year she goes to the synagogue on Spasoglinishchevsky Lane without announcement, and finds the street impassable: tens of thousands of Soviet Jews have come to look at her, and they will not disperse, and they call her by her first name. She says almost nothing. Stalin's answer begins within months, with arrests.
suggested_refs: The Moscow Choral Synagogue, 10 Bolshoy Spasoglinishchevsky Lane
The Israeli 10,000-shekel banknote of November 1984, which carried her portrait beside the image of that crowd

stops.name: Jerusalem, sworn into the First Knesset and given Labour
stops.date_confidence: The First Knesset was sworn in on 14 February 1949, not 12 February as an earlier dossier had it, and it met that day in the Jewish Agency building in Jerusalem before moving to Tel Aviv and later to Froumine House; the pin is therefore the Jewish Agency, not the Givat Ram building dedicated in 1966. Her appointment as Minister of Labour and National Insurance on 10 March 1949 is attested by the MSU Denver chronology and the Jewish Virtual Library. Her continuous Knesset service ran to 3 June 1974.
stops.campa: She is recalled from Moscow, elected on the Mapai list, and given Labour and National Insurance in the first government, which is the ministry nobody fights for and the one the arriving hundreds of thousands actually meet. The country doubles its population in three years. She builds thirty thousand units of housing, roads to put the new immigrants to work, and a national insurance scheme. In the Knesset she defends the tent camps and the tin huts of the maabarot against her own side. The alternative on offer is a quota on who may come.
suggested_refs: The maabarot transit camps of 1949-1952 and the Ministry of Labour's housing programme

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the mayoralty refused her
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia dates the episode to the summer of 1955 and records that she lost by two votes, with religious councillors voting against her; the MSU Denver chronology gives the same episode without the margin. The coordinate is the old municipality on Bialik Square, where the council sat in 1955; the current city hall on Rabin Square, used in an earlier dossier, only opened in 1965. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Mapai puts her name forward for mayor of Tel Aviv and the council votes her down by two, the religious members declining to install a woman over the city. She has run the Labour ministry for six years by then, built its housing, drafted its insurance law, and defended its budget line by line. She will be Foreign Minister of the country within the year. Morris died in 1951 and her mother in the same year. She is living alone in a Tel Aviv flat and has not furnished it.
suggested_refs: The old Tel Aviv city hall on Bialik Square and the municipal council vote of summer 1955

stops.name: Jerusalem, the ministry and the shortened name
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Foreign Minister from 18 June 1956 to 12 January 1966 (Wikipedia, Golda Meir), corroborated in outline by the Jewish Virtual Library, which dates the tenure June 1956 to January 1966. She left the Labour ministry on 19 June 1956, the day after taking Foreign Affairs. The Hebraisation of Meyerson to Meir at Ben-Gurion's instruction is attested by the MSU Denver chronology. The Foreign Ministry's premises are not pinned in any source reachable here, so the coordinate is Jerusalem.
stops.campa: Ben-Gurion moves her to Foreign Affairs and tells her, as he tells the rest of the diplomatic service, to take a Hebrew name. Meyerson becomes Meir, which means illuminates. She takes over a ministry of professionals who resent her arrival, speaks no French, and reads no cables in the original. The file nobody else wants is Africa, and her argument for taking it is that a country poor eight years ago can teach what it has just learned. She sends agronomists and irrigation engineers, trains nurses from Ghana and Tanzania, and keeps the programme running for seven years.
suggested_refs: The Israeli technical assistance programmes in newly independent Africa, 1958-1965

stops.name: Sevres, the villa outside Paris
stops.date_confidence: The secret tripartite coordination preceding the Sinai campaign was the Sevres conference of 22-24 October 1956, held at a villa in Sevres outside Paris, not in Paris and not in the Sinai as an earlier dossier had it. That Meir participated in the secret Israeli, French and British coordination is stated by the MSU Denver chronology; no source reachable here itemizes the Israeli delegation at Sevres, so her presence in that room specifically is reconstruction. The pin is the town of Sevres, not the villa.
stops.campa: In a suburban villa southwest of Paris, over three days, an Israeli party, a French party and a British party write down a war and agree to deny that the document exists: Israel will attack in the Sinai, Britain and France will demand that both sides withdraw from the canal, and Egypt's refusal will supply the pretext for a landing. Copies are made and destroyed unevenly. Israel takes the peninsula in a week and is made to give it back within months. Out of the arrangement comes a French reactor at Dimona.
suggested_refs: The Protocol of Sevres, 24 October 1956

stops.name: Jerusalem, the grenade in the chamber
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia (Golda Meir) records that in the grenade attack on the Knesset chamber of 29 October 1957 Meir's foot was slightly injured; she was present and among the wounded, alongside Ben-Gurion. An earlier dossier hedged on whether she was in the chamber, which the source refutes. The chamber in 1957 was Froumine House on King George Street, occupied from 1950 until the Givat Ram building was dedicated on 30 August 1966; the pin is an approximation for Froumine House and was not landmark-verified in a source reachable here.
stops.campa: A man in the public gallery drops a Mills bomb into the Knesset while the government sits below. Ben-Gurion is hit in the leg, the religious affairs minister is badly wounded, and the Foreign Minister's foot is torn open by a fragment. The chamber is a converted bank building on King George Street, the plenum on the ground floor, the country's whole parliament inside it. She is back at her desk within days. The Knesset will not have a building of its own for another nine years.
suggested_refs: Froumine House, King George Street, Jerusalem, seat of the Knesset 1950-1966

stops.name: Jerusalem, the letter to the ambassador in Warsaw
stops.date_confidence: The letter is attested and its text reproduced: Golda Meir to Katriel Katz, Israel's ambassador to Poland, 1958, printed by JTA on 9 December 2009 from the letter's discovery by Professor Szymon Rudnicki. This is the clearest paper trail to a primary document in the whole research pool. The month and day of the letter are not given and default to 01; the ministry premises are not pinned, so the coordinate is Jerusalem.
stops.campa: As Foreign Minister she writes to Israel's ambassador in Warsaw about the Polish aliyah, and asks him to find out whether the Polish government can be told that Israel wishes to institute selection, because sick and handicapped immigrants cannot go on being accepted. A decade earlier the same woman defended the maabarot in the Knesset against a quota on who may come. The letter is on ministry paper and is signed. It lies in an archive for fifty-one years. Szymon Rudnicki finds it in Warsaw in 2009 and JTA prints the text that December.
stops.quote: A proposal was raised in the coordination committee to inform the Polish government that we want to institute selection in aliyah, because we cannot continue accepting sick and handicapped people. Please give your opinion as to whether this can be explained to the Poles without hurting immigration.
stops.quote_source: Golda Meir, letter to Israel's ambassador to Poland Katriel Katz, 1958, printed in JTA, 9 December 2009
suggested_refs: The Meir-Katz letter of 1958, published by JTA on 9 December 2009 after its discovery by Szymon Rudnicki
sources: JTA, 9 December 2009, 'Meir letter on immigrant selection'

stops.name: New York, the Security Council and the man in the glass box
stops.date_confidence: Her address to the United Nations Security Council concerning the capture of Adolf Eichmann is attested by the MSU Denver chronology, which gives 1960 without a date; month and day default to 01. The Council met at United Nations headquarters in New York, which is the pin. The Argentine complaint that produced the debate was lodged in June 1960; the sources reachable here do not fix the day of her speech.
stops.campa: Israeli agents take Adolf Eichmann out of a suburb of Buenos Aires and fly him to Tel Aviv, and Argentina complains to the Security Council that its sovereignty has been violated, which it has. She goes to New York to answer for it. The argument she makes is not legal, because the legal argument is bad: she tells the Council what Eichmann organised and how many, and that no court had been able to reach him in fifteen years. The Council votes censure. Nobody asks for him back.
suggested_refs: United Nations Security Council Resolution 138 of 23 June 1960 on the Eichmann case

stops.name: Tel Aviv, leaving the ministry with a diagnosis in her pocket
stops.date_confidence: Departure from the Foreign Ministry in January 1966 citing exhaustion, and her election as secretary-general of Mapai and then of the merged Labour Party, are attested by the MSU Denver chronology; the tenure ended 12 January 1966 (Wikipedia). The lymphoma diagnosis is contested: the MSU Denver chronology gives 1963, while a separately reported account places it in late 1965. No primary medical record is reachable here, and the year is left unresolved. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: She resigns the Foreign Ministry at sixty-seven, telling the party she is tired, which is true and is not the whole of it: she has lymphoma, treated in secret, and will be treated in secret for another twelve years while the country reads about her fatigue. Whether the diagnosis came in 1963 or in late 1965 the sources do not agree. She takes the party secretariat instead, and spends four years welding Mapai, Ahdut HaAvoda and Rafi into one Labour Party.
suggested_refs: The merger of Mapai, Ahdut HaAvoda and Rafi into the Israeli Labour Party, 1968

stops.name: Jerusalem, sworn in as a compromise
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Levi Eshkol died on 26 February 1969 and Meir became Prime Minister on 17 March 1969, chosen by the Labour central committee as a compromise candidate (MSU Denver chronology; Jewish Virtual Library). The coordinate is the Knesset at Givat Ram, confirmed by Wikipedia (Knesset), which had been the seat since 30 August 1966.
stops.campa: Levi Eshkol dies in office and the party cannot choose between Dayan and Allon, so it sends for the retired secretary-general, seventy years old, undergoing treatment she has told no one about, and installs her while it decides properly. She takes the office on the seventeenth of March. She governs by convening a handful of ministers in her own kitchen over tea and cigarettes until they agree, then bringing the agreement to the cabinet already made. The arrangement is nicknamed the kitchen cabinet.
suggested_refs: The Knesset at Givat Ram, dedicated 30 August 1966

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Black Panthers at the door
stops.date_confidence: The meeting with leaders of the Israeli Black Panthers on 13 April 1971 is attested by the MSU Denver chronology. The venue is not fixed by any source reachable here, so the pin is city-level Jerusalem rather than a named building. Her reported remark afterwards, that they were not nice, is widely quoted in Israeli accounts but was not verified against a primary transcript in this research.
stops.campa: Young men from Musrara, children of families brought from Morocco and Iraq and settled in the worst housing the state had, take the name of the American Black Panthers and demonstrate in Jerusalem over jobs, schooling and police treatment. She agrees to receive their leaders on the thirteenth of April and the meeting goes badly on both sides: they arrive angry and she treats them as delinquents. No transcript of it has been produced. The sentence the country quotes from the room afterwards, that they were not nice, has never been checked against one.
suggested_refs: The Israeli Black Panther movement of Musrara, Jerusalem, 1971

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Mitchell Theatre, a Yiddish comedy
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The whole of the evidence is Bruce Oppenheimer's recollection to Veronica Belling, which places a performance by the Yiddish comedian Max Perelman at the Mitchell Theatre in Jerusalem around 1971 or 1972, with Meir in the audience. No programme, press notice or security record has been produced, the venue's address was not independently located, and the pin is the Jerusalem city coordinate inherited from the Perelman file. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: The Prime Minister comes into a Jerusalem theatre after the lights are down, with a thin detail, and takes a seat in the stalls to watch a Yiddish comedy. Her own government has spent twenty years discouraging exactly this, on the grounds that the language of the diaspora competes with Hebrew and ought to be allowed to die. She was born in Kyiv and Yiddish was her first language, as it was the first language of most of the room. Max Perelman is sixty-two and has been refining the same act since Riga.
stops.quote: I sat upstairs and I recall that Golda Meir who was Prime Minister at the time, came in after lights out, with a meagre security detail and sat in front of me. I was so excited and happy to be in the same space as her, watching Yiddish theatre.
stops.quote_source: Bruce Oppenheimer, recollection to Veronica Belling, quoted in Belling, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 2020
suggested_refs: The Mitchell Theatre, Jerusalem, c. 1971-1972

stops.name: Jerusalem, the cabinet after Munich
stops.date_confidence: The Munich hostage crisis of September 1972 is attested, as is her authorisation of covert retaliatory operations afterwards (MSU Denver chronology). Meir was in Israel, not in Munich, and the stop is placed where she was; the cabinet venue is not fixed in the sources reachable here. Her sister Sheyna Korngold died in 1972 (Wikipedia gives her dates as 1889-1972). The claim that Meir was elected deputy chairman of the Socialist International in the same year appears in no source reachable here and is dropped.
stops.campa: Eleven Israeli athletes are taken hostage at the Olympic Games and killed at a German airfield during a rescue that fails in the dark. She had asked Bonn to let Israeli units handle it and had been refused. Afterwards she authorises a standing programme of killings abroad, run by the Mossad against the men held responsible, and it will go on for years and will kill a Moroccan waiter in Norway by mistake. Her sister Sheyna, the one who took her in at Denver, dies the same year at eighty-three.
suggested_refs: The Munich Olympics hostage crisis of 5-6 September 1972 and the operations authorised after it

stops.name: Washington, at the White House with Nixon
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia (Golda Meir) gives her meetings with Nixon as 1969 and 1 March 1973. An earlier dossier dated the second to 28 February 1973; she was in Washington from late February, but the meeting itself was on 1 March. The pin is the White House; some associated meetings, including those with Kissinger, took place at venues not specified in the sources reachable here.
stops.campa: She comes to Washington to ask for Phantom aircraft and gets a hearing that is warmer in the room than on paper. It is the second time the two of them have met, the first having been in 1969, his first year in the office and hers. Nixon likes her and Kissinger, who is Secretary of State in waiting and a Jew from Furth, negotiates with her as with a rival rather than a supplicant. Seven months later the same three people will be on the telephone at night over an airlift. The terms of that conversation are set here, in March.
suggested_refs: The Meir-Nixon meeting of 1 March 1973

stops.name: Vienna, the closed transit camp
stops.date_confidence: The Schoenau hostage-taking is dated to September 1973 and the Vienna meeting with Chancellor Bruno Kreisky to a few days later (Wikipedia, Golda Meir), that is, early October 1973 and not within September as an earlier dossier had it; the meeting is commonly given as 2 October, which is used here. The pin is Vienna city, no venue being named in the sources reachable here.
stops.campa: Palestinian gunmen seize a train carrying Soviet Jewish emigrants at the Austrian border, and Kreisky ends the hostage affair by agreeing to close the Schoenau castle transit facility through which those emigrants have been passing to Israel. She flies to Vienna to argue him out of it and he does not move; two Jews, one a Chancellor, disagreeing across a table about what Austria owes. She leaves having got nothing. The war starts four days later.
suggested_refs: The Schoenau castle transit facility for Soviet Jewish emigrants, closed after the attack of 28 September 1973

segments.name: The War, the Commission, the Hill

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the morning of the sixth of October
stops.date_confidence: The war opened on 6 October 1973 with a coordinated Egyptian and Syrian attack (MSU Denver chronology). Two things about the scene are unresolved. The venue is contested: an earlier dossier placed the morning consultations at the Prime Minister's residence in Jerusalem, whose own coordinate it also gave wrongly, while the conventional placing is her office in the Kirya in Tel Aviv, which is used here as an approximate pin. The decisions themselves rest on published record and on FRUS and National Security Archive material that was not independently fetched in this research.
stops.campa: At dawn she is told the attack will come that day. David Elazar wants full mobilisation and a pre-emptive air strike; Moshe Dayan wants a partial call-up and no strike at all. She takes the larger mobilisation and refuses the strike, on the reasoning that Israel must be seen to be hit first or Washington will not resupply it. Four hours later two armies cross the lines. Within a week the Americans are flying in equipment. Was the strike she refused the one that would have held the canal? Every commission and every memoir since has answered it differently.
suggested_refs: Declassified documents on the October 1973 war, National Security Archive Electronic Briefing Book 98
William Gibson's play Golda's Balcony, 2003, which dramatises a nuclear ultimatum that the declassified record does not support
sources: National Security Archive, Electronic Briefing Book 98

stops.name: Jerusalem, the commission and the resignation
stops.date_confidence: Both dates in an earlier dossier were off by a day: Wikipedia gives the resignation announcement as 11 April 1974 and her departure from office as 3 June 1974, when Rabin's government took office. Her testimony to the Agranat Commission is attested in outline; the hearing venue is not independently confirmed and the pin is the Knesset. The commission's interim report of April 1974 cleared the political level and censured the military, which is what made the political level untenable.
stops.campa: The Agranat Commission takes evidence through the winter on how the intelligence services read the Egyptian build-up as an exercise, and in April it censures the Chief of Staff and the head of military intelligence and clears the Prime Minister. The street does not accept the acquittal. Reservists back from the canal demonstrate outside her office; a bereaved father keeps a vigil at the gate. On the eleventh of April she tells the party she has had enough, and on the third of June she hands the government to Yitzhak Rabin.
suggested_refs: The Agranat Commission interim report, April 1974

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the terms of the memoir
stops.date_confidence: My Life was published in 1975 (MSU Denver chronology) and became a New York Times bestseller (Wikipedia). The quotation given here is the complete sentence pair as printed on the MSU Denver chronology page under 1975; an earlier dossier appended a trailing ellipsis that is not in the source and falsely implied omitted material. Where she wrote is not documented in the sources reachable here, and the pin is Tel Aviv. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Out of office at seventy-seven, she agrees with the publisher George Weidenfeld to write the book, and sets the terms before the contract: nothing about her private life, no scores settled. My Life comes out in 1975 and sells enormously. It is warm, plain, unrevealing, and silent on the marriage, on the men, and on the cancer she is still being treated for. It stops short of the war. What it does answer, it answers in the words she used in the Knesset.
stops.quote: I will not write about my private life. I will not settle political or other scores with anyone.
stops.quote_source: Golda Meir to her publisher George Weidenfeld, quoted on the MSU Denver chronology page under 1975
suggested_refs: Golda Meir, My Life (Weidenfeld and Nicolson, 1975)

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Knesset on the day after Sadat
stops.date_confidence: Her speech of 21 November 1977 is attested, but the occasion is commonly misdescribed. Anwar Sadat's visit ran 19 to 21 November 1977 and his address to the Knesset was on 20 November (Wikipedia, Anwar Sadat's visit to Israel); Meir spoke the following day, in the debate that continued after it. She did not speak during his address, and an earlier dossier collapsed the two days.
stops.campa: The President of Egypt lands at Ben Gurion airport, is received by the men whose armies he attacked four years earlier, and speaks to the Knesset. She is a private citizen and is called to the chamber for the debate the next day, and she stands up and addresses him as an old lady, which is the word she uses, and calls him courageous, and says she hopes the grandchildren will be spared what the parents had. Sadat calls her the old lady in return. He is assassinated four years later; she is dead within thirteen months.
suggested_refs: The Knesset debate of 21 November 1977, following Sadat's address of 20 November

stops.name: Ein Karem, the twelve secret years end
stops.date_confidence: Death on 8 December 1978 in West Jerusalem is attested (Wikipedia). Three specifics are not: the hospitalisation on 7 December, the time of 4.30 in the afternoon, and the naming of Hadassah Ein Kerem as the hospital rest on the MSU Denver chronology alone, and no source reachable here corroborates them. The pin follows that attribution to the Ein Karem hilltop, roughly 31.766 north 35.150 east; note that the Hadassah article's own infobox coordinate is the Mount Scopus campus and misleads anyone deriving it there.
stops.campa: She dies of lymphoma at eighty, twelve years after the country was told she was merely tired, and the hospital announces the illness only once she is dead. The treatment had gone on quietly through the party secretariat, the premiership, the war, the commission and the memoir, and none of those pages mentions it. She had gone on smoking through all of it. The chronology naming the hospital and the hour of half past four is a single American university page, and nothing else reachable corroborates either. What is fixed is the date and the city.
suggested_refs: Hadassah Ein Kerem Medical Centre, on the hilltop above Ein Karem, West Jerusalem

stops.name: Mount Herzl, the plot of the leaders
stops.date_confidence: Burial on Mount Herzl in the Great Leaders of the Nation plot is attested (Wikipedia, Mount Herzl), and the coordinate is that article's, correcting an earlier dossier that was 330 m off. The burial date of 12 December is given by the MSU Denver chronology alone and is not corroborated in any source reachable here. The neighbouring graves in the plot are attested: Eshkol, Rabin, Shazar, Herzog, Peres, Sprinzak, Kaplan and Kollek.
stops.campa: She is buried on the hillside plot kept for prime ministers and presidents, beside Levi Eshkol, whose death made her Prime Minister, and near where Yitzhak Rabin, who took the government from her hands in June 1974, will be laid seventeen years later. The funeral is plain at her own instruction. The date given for the burial, the twelfth of December, rests on one American university chronology and is corroborated nowhere reachable. The plot fills in around her over the decades that follow: Shazar, Herzog, Peres, Sprinzak, Kaplan, Kollek.
suggested_refs: The Great Leaders of the Nation plot, Mount Herzl, Jerusalem
